lessons.title: Explain it line by line
lessons.goal: You can pair every line of a piece of code with your own explanation and list the lines you cannot explain yet.
lessons.theory:
Programmers have an old trick called **rubber duck debugging**: you explain your code, line by line, to a rubber duck on your desk. The duck says nothing, but halfway through you often hear yourself say "wait, that is wrong".

With AI-written code this habit is the minimum. Before you use a snippet, you should be able to say what **every** line does. A line you cannot explain is a line you cannot fix when it breaks, and you are the one who will have to fix it.

You can make this a small routine in Python. Split the code into lines, then walk through them with a number:

```python
code_lines = snippet.split("\n")
for number, line in enumerate(code_lines, start=1):
    print(number, line)
```

`enumerate(..., start=1)` gives you the line number and the line together, counting from 1 like a code editor does.

Keep your explanations in a dict keyed by line number. `my_notes.get(number, "???")` returns your note, or `"???"` when there is none, without crashing. The lines that end up with no note are exactly the ones to study, or to ask the AI about, before you trust the code.

lessons.title: Measure your own progress
lessons.goal: You can use simple statistics on your weekly results to see whether you are really improving on your own.
lessons.theory:
Feelings are a poor measure of progress. Some weeks you feel stuck and are actually improving; other weeks everything feels easy because an AI did the hard part. Numbers help you see what is really happening.

Two numbers are worth tracking each week:

- your quiz **score**, from quizzes on your own notes
- how many tasks you solved **alone**, out of all the tasks you did

The `statistics` module does the maths:

import statistics

scores = [55, 63, 60, 74]
avg = statistics.mean(scores)
print(f"Average score: {avg:.1f}")   # 63.0

`max(scores)` gives the best score, and `scores[-1] - scores[0]` shows how far you moved from the first week to the last.

For the share of tasks done alone, divide and turn it into a percentage: `round(100 * alone / tasks)` gives a whole number like `83`.

Read the two numbers together. A rising score with a falling "alone" share means the tool is doing more of the work, not you. The healthy sign is both going up: you still use AI, but you need it less for the same kind of task.

lessons.theory:
In this chapter you build one small program across eight missions: a **study assistant**. You ask it a question, and it works like this:

- it finds the notes of **yours** that match the question

lessons.title: Scoring notes by keywords
lessons.goal: You can score each note by how many words of a question it contains.
lessons.theory:
To find the notes that fit a question, you need a way to measure "fits". A simple, clear rule: **count how many words of the question appear in the note**.

First, turn text into a list of words. The starter has a `words(text)` helper for that:

```python
found = re.findall(r"[a-z]+", text.lower())
```

`re.findall` returns every run of letters, so `"KeyError!"` becomes `["keyerror"]`. The helper also drops tiny words such as "how", "a" and "the" (the `STOP` list). They appear everywhere and would make every note look relevant.

Then the score of a note is a count:

```python
total = 0
for w in words(question):
    if w in note_words:
        total += 1
```

Look at the title and the text together, since a title often holds the best keyword.

This is a crude rule, and it is good to know its limits. `"avoid"` does not match `"avoids"`, and a note can score by pure chance. Real systems use smarter matching, but the idea is the same: rank what you have, then give the best pieces to the model. A rule you fully understand is a good first version.

lessons.title: Picking the top notes
lessons.goal: You can sort notes by score and keep only the best matches.
lessons.theory:
Now that every note has a score, pick the best ones. You do not send every note to the model. Fewer, better notes keep the prompt short and the answer focused, and a real model has a limit on how much text it can read at once.

`sorted` can sort by any rule you give it with `key`. A **lambda** is a tiny one-line function, handy for exactly this:

ranked = sorted(notes, key=lambda n: score(n, question),

lessons.title: Reading the model's JSON reply
lessons.goal: You can turn a model's reply into a dict safely and reject replies that are broken or incomplete.
lessons.theory:
You asked the model for JSON. Most of the time you get it. Sometimes you get a friendly sentence in front of it, or a key is missing. Your program must never crash on a bad reply, and it must never use a half-correct one as if it were fine.

In this mission the replies are **stand-ins** written in the starter: plain strings shaped like what a real model sends back.

`json.loads(raw)` turns JSON text into Python data. If the text is not valid JSON, it raises `json.JSONDecodeError`, so wrap it in `try`:

```python
try:
    data = json.loads(raw)
except json.JSONDecodeError:
    return None
```

Valid JSON is still not enough. Check the shape too:

- `isinstance(data, dict)` is `True` only when the reply is a dict (and not, say, a list or a number)
- both keys, `"answer"` and `"note_ids"`, must be in it

If any check fails, return `None`. The caller then knows that this reply cannot be used. Returning `None` in one clear place is simpler and safer than letting a `KeyError` pop up three functions later.

import re

data = [
    ("Slices",

    ("Dict get",
     "d.get(key, default) avoids a KeyError when a key is missing."),
    ("Try and except",

    ("Append",
     "append adds one item to the end of a list, in place."),
    ("Random seed",
     "random.seed(n) makes random results repeat every run."),
]

def add_note(notes, title, text):
    note = {"id": len(notes) + 1, "title": title, "text": text}
    notes.append(note)
    return note

notes = []
for title, text in data:
    add_note(notes, title, text)

STOP = ["how", "do", "i", "a", "an", "the", "is", "in",
        "when", "what", "to", "of", "my", "it"]

def words(text):
    found = re.findall(r"[a-z]+", text.lower())
    result = []
    for w in found:
        if w not in STOP:
            result.append(w)
    return result

def score(note, question):
    note_words = words(note["title"] + " " + note["text"])
    total = 0
    for w in words(question):
        if w in note_words:
            total += 1
    return total

def top_notes(notes, question, k=2):
    ranked = sorted(notes, key=lambda n: score(n, question),
                    reverse=True)
    chosen = []
    for note in ranked:
        if score(note, question) > 0:
            chosen.append(note)
    return chosen[:k]

HEADER = [
    "Answer using only the notes below.",
    "If the notes do not cover it, say so.",
    'Reply in JSON: {"answer": "...", "note_ids": [1]}',
]

def build_prompt(question, chosen):

    for note in chosen:
        lines.append(f"[{note['id']}] {note['title']}: {note['text']}")
    lines.append("")
    lines.append("Question: " + question)
    return "\n".join(lines)

lessons.title: Checking the answer with small tests
lessons.goal: You can write checks that catch a model reply citing notes it never saw or ignoring its notes.
lessons.theory:
A reply that is valid JSON can still be wrong. Before you trust it, run a few small, automatic checks. You cannot check everything, but two cheap tests catch common problems:

- **Invented sources.** The reply says it used note 7, but you only sent notes 2 and 3. A model can make up a citation that looks real. Any id that was not sent is a red flag.
- **Ignored context.** The answer shares no words at all with the notes you sent. Then it probably came from somewhere else, not from your notes.

Collect problems in a list instead of stopping at the first one, so you see everything that is wrong at once:

```python
problems = []
if n not in sent:
    problems.append(f"cites note {n}, which was not sent")
```

An empty list means every check passed.

For the second check you can reuse `score`: `score(note, reply["answer"])` counts the answer's words that appear in a note. Add that up over the chosen notes. If the total is 0, the answer ignored them.

The starter also has `note_ids(chosen)`, which returns the ids of the chosen notes as a list, like `[2, 3]`.

Passing these checks does not prove the answer is true. It proves that it is **worth reading**. You still read it.

lessons.title: A safety filter before sending
lessons.goal: You can hide emails and phone numbers in a prompt and block a prompt that contains a secret.
lessons.theory:
Everything in a prompt leaves your computer when you send it to a real model. People paste emails, phone numbers and even passwords into questions without noticing. So the last step before sending is a **safety filter**, in code, every time. Code does not forget.

The filter does two different jobs:

- **Redact** personal data: replace it with a label, so the question still makes sense without it.
- **Block** secrets: some things should never be sent at all, not even hidden.

`re.sub(pattern, replacement, text)` replaces every match of a pattern:

```python
text = re.sub(EMAIL, "[EMAIL]", text)
```

The starter has the patterns ready. `EMAIL` matches things like `ana.lopez@example.com`, and `PHONE` matches numbers like `555 123 4567`.

Blocking is simpler: if any word from `BLOCKED` appears in the lowercased prompt, it is not safe to send. Redacting a password is not enough. A hidden password was still typed into a place it did not belong, so the right answer is to stop and tell the user.

Run the filter on the **whole prompt**, not only the question. Your notes could hold private data too.

lessons.title: The final run
lessons.goal: You can connect every piece into one assistant that finds notes, filters, asks, checks and reports.
lessons.theory:
Time to connect everything. Each piece does one job, and the order matters:

- **find** the top notes, and stop if none match
- **build** the prompt and **redact** it
- **block** it if it holds a secret, before anything is sent
- **ask** the model, then **parse** the reply
- **check** the reply, then report

`fake_model(prompt)` in the starter is a **stand-in** for a real model call. It returns canned JSON text and never touches the network. In a real tool, only that one line would change. Everything around it (the filter before, the checks after) stays exactly the same, and that is the part that makes the tool trustworthy.

Each early stop returns a short status word, so the caller can count results:

```python
if not safe_to_send(prompt):
    print("Blocked: the prompt holds a secret.")
    return "blocked"
```

Notice what the report tells you. One question passed. One was blocked on purpose. One had no notes, which tells you what to study next. One reply cited a note that was never sent, and the check caught it. A tool that shows you its failures is one you can trust. A tool that always says "done" is one you have to check by hand.
